title: An Anchor Does Not Hold a Ship by Being Heavy
hook: How does a ten ton anchor hold a fifty thousand ton ship?
loop: Ends on 'when a ship of fifty thousand tons rides out a storm on ten tons of steel,' handing back into scene 2. Pattern A.

scenes.text: A ship weighing fifty thousand tons is being held in place by an anchor that weighs ten.
So is the anchor simply enormous? Heavy enough to pin a steel island to the seabed?
On its own, an anchor that size would skate across the bottom like a stone.
The holding power was never really in the anchor. It is in the chain.
Crews pay out far more chain than the water is deep. Often five to seven times more.
In thirty metres of water, that can mean two hundred metres of chain.
Most of it never hangs. It lies flat along the seabed.
And that is the whole trick.
The weight of the chain keeps the pull on the anchor horizontal instead of upward.
Pulled sideways, the flukes bite in and drag themselves deeper.
Pulled upward, the same anchor pops free instantly.
But the chain is doing something else as well.
When a wave lifts the bow, the curve of chain on the bottom straightens instead of jerking the anchor.
It works as a spring, absorbing every surge before it ever reaches the seabed.
Let out too little chain, and that curve disappears. The pull turns upward, and the anchor starts to drag.
Which is how a ship of fifty thousand tons rides out a storm
